name: Hunde
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mateene, Kahombo C. 1967. Le changement des phonèmes du hunde à partir du système phonologique du proto-bantou. Africana Linguistica 3 (Annales du Musée Royal de l'Afrique Centrale, Sciences humaines 61): 65-78. Tervuren. DOI 10.3406/aflin.1967.872 (open access on Persée).
catalog_locator: p. 67 (Note préliminaire) and pp. 69-70, §3 'Phonèmes supra-segmentaux', §§3.1-3.2 with footnote 3 (Persée page views T1_67, T1_69, T1_70); the 'semi-longue' sentence is on p. 70.
catalog_quote: les tons du proto-bantou sont maintenus en hunde, cependant que la valeur phonologique de la quantité vocalique semble perdue. ... 3.1 Notre manque de temps et l'absence dans l'état actuel du H. de voyelle ou de consonne dont la longueur ait une valeur phonologique (distinctive) nous autorisent de ne pas considérer pour le moment la question de l'éventuel réflexe en H. de la quantité des phonèmes du P.B. Phonétiquement, la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde. 3.2 Sur le plan tonologique, les données du H. semblent, dans la majorité des cas, confirmer les reconstructions de Greenberg. ... Le ton haut est noté au moyen d'un accent aigu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Hunde (hund1239) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Philippson 1991 (542-pp. Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East African Bantu), was already held by the project from today's bemb1257 pass (author's PDF from ddl.cnrs.fr, URL confirmed live); a byte-identical copy and four page extracts are now under and. Read in full for Hunde: Table 1 p. 70 lists Hunde (D51) as a poorly-known group-I language; pp. 412-413 say only that Hunde has reduced Proto-Bantu HH to HB in isolation forms (mukátsi, Ngóko, -kúlu vs kubóko, muhíni), citing Mateene 1967 as its sole Hunde source (p. 516); the penultimate/accent typology (pp. 483-485) does not mention Hunde. classification: tone language, silent on word stress; relevance prosody-but-not-word-stress; priority none. The only first-hand penultimate-prominence statement read is Mateene 1967 p. 70 ('la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde'), a phonetic half-length remark, not a stress claim (missed in the earlier reading, now noted). Mateene 1992 grammar, Kaji 1992 vocabulary introduction, Goldsmith 1985 'Tone in KiHunde' and Murairi Mitima 2008 remain unread (print/CDL only) and would be the places to look for an explicit Hunde stress statement.

new_statements.quote: Notre manque de temps et l'absence dans l'état actuel du H. de voyelle ou de consonne dont la longueur ait une valeur phonologique (distinctive) nous autorisent de ne pas considérer pour le moment la question de l'éventuel réflexe en H. de la quantité des phonèmes du P.B. Phonétiquement, la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde.
new_statements.translation: Our lack of time and the absence, in the present state of Hunde, of any vowel or consonant whose length has phonological (distinctive) value allow us not to consider for now the question of a possible Hunde reflex of Proto-Bantu phoneme quantity. Phonetically, the vowel of every pre-final [penultimate] syllable is realized half-long in Hunde.
new_statements.citation: Mateene, Kahombo C. 1967. Le changement des phonèmes du hunde à partir du système phonologique du proto-bantou. Africana Linguistica 3 (Annales MRAC, Sciences humaines 61): 65-78. DOI 10.3406/aflin.1967.872 (open access on Persée).
new_statements.reading: First-hand (native-speaker linguist) statement that Hunde has no phonological length and that every penultimate syllable carries phonetic half-length; it is a penultimate-prominence (lengthening) statement, not an explicit stress/accent claim, and the same author treats Hunde as a tone language (§3.2, Proto-Bantu tones largely preserved). Consistent with Bastin 2003 (Bantu Languages ch. 25, p. 505: Hunde length limited to the penultimate vowel at utterance end). Note: the earlier line for this article said 'Stress: nothing'; this sentence was missed then and is now recorded there. Philippson 1991 (the works with stress in the title) adds nothing on stress for Hunde. No source read in this search of works with stress in the title states word stress for Hunde; if the catalog codes Hunde, the available evidence supports 'tone language with phonetic penultimate lengthening; no stress statement in the literature read'.

tone_statements.citation: Goldsmith, John A. 1990. Autosegmental and Metrical Phonology. Oxford & Cambridge, MA: Basil Blackwell. (KiHunde: sect. 1.7 'The Conjunctivity Condition', pp. 36-40; ch. 3 'Syllable structure', pp. 162-165; notes 11, 47.) ISBN 0-631-13675-4.
tone_statements.quote: Our final example of a Bantu tone system comes from KiHunde, a language spoken in eastern Zaire.11 Every morpheme in KiHunde (except the verbal extensions) has either a Low tone or a High tone. No single vowel can bear more than one tone, and although vowels can be long or short underlyingly, on the surface the only vowel chat can be long is the vowel in the penultimate syllable of the phrase. It follows, then, that only in penultimate position can a contour tone appear on the surface, since contour tones are sequences of level tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 36, sect. 1.7 'The Conjunctivity Condition', opening paragraph
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (H, L); surface contours only on phrase-penultimate long vowel

tone_statements.quote: In each of these languages, a pattern of tones is spread over the stem of the verb, a pattern which is determined in part by the lexical tone, High or Low, of the verb radical, and in part by the tense of the verb as a whole. ... Also to be included in the Interlacustrine group are MaShi, analyzed by Louise Polak-Bynon, and KiHunde, analyzed by myself (Goldsmith to appear a); both languages are spoken in eastern Zaire. ... (5) High tone radical (KiHunde) tu na [ tém er an á "we cut for each other" Low tone radical tu na [ som ér an a "we read for each other"
tone_statements.summary: Verb radicals lexically High or Low; tenses add High tone suffixes to the 2nd stem vowel and/or Final Vowel, lowered by Meeussen's Rule (H->L / H__); extensions toneless. Downstep noted only for Shi.

sources.citation: Philippson, Gérard (1991 [defended 1992]). Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V (René Descartes), dir. J.M.C. Thomas. 542 pp. NNT 1992PA05H011. Glottolog ref 38907 (listed by Glottolog as an overview; comparative; study of one feature).
sources.quote: p. 412-413: "Dans le groupe I, le fuliru est proche du shi et présente probablement les mêmes oppositions que ce dernier. Le hunde, par contre, si l'on s'en tient aux formes en isolation, a réduit HH à HB : muk&atsi, "femme", Ng&oko, "poulet", -k&ulu, "vieux"; cf. kub&oko, "bras", muh&Kni, "manche", etc. La tendance à cette réduction se ferait donc déjà sentir dans le groupe I." [& marks H on the following vowel in the author's font encoding]. Table 1 p. 70 lists "hunde (D 51)" in group I with no cross, i.e. among the languages "mal connus, voire totalement inconnus". English: "In group I, Fuliru is close to Shi and probably shows the same oppositions as the latter. Hunde, by contrast, if one keeps to isolation forms, has reduced HH to HB: mukátsi 'woman', Ngóko 'chicken', -kúlu 'old'; cf. kubóko 'arm', muhíni 'handle', etc. The tendency toward this reduction would thus already be felt in group I."
sources.locator: Table 1 p. 70 (p. 70); Ch. 6 §2.1.6 pp. 412-413 (pp. 412-413); Ch. 6 §3.5.2 pp. 483-485; bibliography p. 516; index p. 536 ('hunde; 407; 512' = TOC/index pagination is ~5-7 pp. off the PDF pagination)
sources.note: Nothing about word stress or accent placement in Hunde. Hunde appears only as a poorly-known group-I (D50) member: one diachronic remark that Proto-Bantu HH nominal themes surface as HB in isolation forms (data from Mateene 1967, the thesis's sole Hunde source, bibliography p. 516). The thesis's penultimate/accent typology (Ch. 6 §3.5.2 pp. 483-485, categories a-e) does not place Hunde in any category; group-I neighbours nande/konzo are put in (c) 'culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième' and shi in (d)(I). So Philippson treats Hunde as a tone language and is silent on…
